opus-5.5.text:
Being open to everyone and being accessible to everyone are not quite the same thing.

The Slack community is great, and anyone can join. But when I talked with engineers in China, many of them simply weren't there. Partly it's practical: Slack isn't something most Chinese developers use every day, and access can be unreliable. Their daily working life happens on WeChat, on Zhihu, in Feishu groups. If the community lives somewhere you have to make a special effort to reach, most people won't make that effort, especially for a quick question.

Then there's language, and I don't mean that people can't read English. Most engineers here read English documentation fine. But asking a question in public, in a second language, in front of the core maintainers, is a real psychological barrier. People worry their question is too basic, or that they'll phrase it badly. So they don't ask. They struggle alone, or they fork the code internally and patch it themselves, and the upstream project never hears about their problem.

That last part is what bothered me most. China has a huge number of vLLM users: big internet companies, cloud providers, chip companies, startups doing inference. Many run vLLM in production at very large scale, and they hit real bugs and real performance issues. They also build very good optimizations. But much of that knowledge stayed inside individual companies. It wasn't flowing back to the community, and the community wasn't flowing to them either.

So the goal of the Chinese community was never to split off or build a separate ecosystem. It was more like a bridge. We give people a place where they can ask questions in Chinese, share experiences, and meet each other at offline meetups. Then we help the good stuff go upstream. When someone finds a bug, we encourage them to file the issue. When a company has a useful optimization, we help them turn it into a proper PR. In the other direction, when there's a major new feature or design change upstream, we explain it in Chinese so people understand the reasoning, not just the code.

Open source is about people, not only code. If a large group of active users is effectively disconnected from the project, that's a loss for everyone. The Chinese community was my attempt to close that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says that Chinese engineers may hesitate to ask publicly in English, even when they can read English documentation, describing a language barrier to participating in the vLLM community.

r002.rationale: It says Slack is not something most Chinese developers use daily and access can be unreliable, making the existing channel harder to reach from China.

r003.rationale: It says major companies used vLLM at scale but kept knowledge and fixes internally, so problems and optimizations were not reaching the upstream community.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the Slack community being open to everyone was the problem, in a way. Open doesn't mean accessible. If you're a Chinese engineer who reads documentation fine but feels a little hesitant typing a question in English in front of a few thousand people, you just don't post. You lurk. And then you go to a WeChat group, or Zhihu, or you ask a colleague, and the question never reaches the people who actually wrote the code.

So I was seeing this gap. A huge fraction of vLLM users and contributors are in China, a lot of the inference work and the hardware adaptation is happening here, but the conversations were fragmented. Someone hits a bug on a domestic chip, they solve it in a private group, and three other teams hit the same bug the next week. On the English side, the maintainers had no visibility into what Chinese users were struggling with, and on the Chinese side, people didn't know what was already being discussed upstream.

There's also a practical thing with Slack. It's slow here, sometimes it's just hard to use. People live in WeChat and Feishu. If the community doesn't exist where people already are, it doesn't really exist for them.

And I'll say the honest version too: part of it was that I wanted Chinese developers to feel like they belonged to the project, not just that they were using it. There's a difference between "I'm allowed to join" and "this is my community." A lot of people have ideas, want to contribute, want to review PRs, and the barrier is often just confidence and language. If someone can ask a half-formed question in Chinese, get an answer, and then we help them turn it into an issue or a PR upstream, that's a much better funnel than hoping they'll show up in Slack on their own.

So I didn't see it as competing with Slack. I saw it as a bridge. The goal is always to get things back into the main project, in English, in the open. The Chinese community is just the on-ramp.

r001.rationale: It says Chinese engineers may hesitate to ask questions in English in the Slack community, so their questions never reach maintainers.

r002.rationale: It says Slack is slow and sometimes hard to use in China, which makes the existing channel less accessible to Chinese participants.

r003.rationale: It describes many vLLM users and contributors in China and limited maintainer visibility, but does not identify major Chinese companies’ adoption of vLLM.

astra-6.text:
I think being open to everyone and being easy for everyone to participate in are two different things. The Slack community was open, but if your first language is Chinese, asking a technical question in English can still feel like a barrier. You have to explain the problem, provide context, and follow the discussion. Some people will simply stay silent.

A Chinese-language community lowers that barrier. People can ask questions, share how they’re using vLLM, and help each other in a language they’re comfortable with. The idea is to create a bridge to the broader community: help more people get involved, and make it easier for their feedback and contributions to reach the project.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that asking technical questions in English can be a barrier for Chinese speakers and may keep them from participating in Slack.

r002.rationale: It does not mention practical difficulties accessing or using overseas software from China.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss adoption by major Chinese companies or communication with vLLM maintainers.

sol-6.1.text:
The Slack community was open to everyone, but being able to join and feeling comfortable participating are two different things. For Chinese-speaking users, asking a technical question in English can take extra effort. Some people may follow the discussions but hesitate to ask questions or share what they’ve learned.

I wanted a Chinese-language community to lower that barrier—to give people a place to discuss vLLM, exchange practical experience, and help each other in a language they’re comfortable with. The idea was to help more people participate and, eventually, connect their questions and contributions back to the broader community.

r001.rationale: It says asking technical questions in English takes extra effort and can make Chinese-speaking users hesitate to participate.

r002.rationale: It does not mention difficulties accessing or using overseas software from China.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss major Chinese companies adopting vLLM or their communication with maintainers.
